intro: Chapter 1 gave you the engine of Pāli: a word’s ending tells you its job. Master the eight cases of the masculine -a noun and the present-tense verb, and you can already read and write real sentences.

blocks.html: English shows meaning mostly by word order (“the man sees the dog” ≠ “the dog sees the man”). Pāli shows it by endings. Naro is always the one doing; naraṃ is always the one receiving. That is why word order in Pāli is flexible, and why endings matter so much.

A case is a job a noun can have in a sentence (subject, object, “with”, “from”, “of” …). Pāli has eight. You learned all eight for the most common noun type, masculine nouns in -a, with nara (man) as the model.

items: Start with the subject in the Nominative: Naro.
Add the object or goal in the Accusative: gāmaṃ.
Add extras, each in its own case: rathena (with a chariot), nagarā (from the city), vihārasmiṃ (in the monastery), mātulassa (of / for the uncle).
Finish with the verb, matching the subject’s number: gacchati.

items.english: The man goes to the village.
The men go to the village by chariot.

items: The verb comes last, and it agrees with the subject in number (-ti / -nti).
Pāli has no “a / the”: naro can be “a man” or “the man”.
The Accusative also marks the goal of motion: gāmaṃ gacchati = “goes to the village”.
Dative and Genitive share -assa and -ānaṃ; context tells “for” from “of”.
The Vocative singular is the bare stem (nara!); its plural equals the Nominative plural.
Neuter nouns differ from masculine only in Nominative, Vocative and Accusative (-aṃ / -āni).

items.english: The man goes to the village by chariot. (Instrumental)
The minister descends from the palace. (Ablative)
The man brings rice for the uncle. (Dative)
The man’s son goes to the village. (Genitive)
The monk sits in the monastery. (Locative)

items.why: A plural subject needs a plural verb ending (-nti).
The place you go to takes the Accusative, not the Nominative.
The thing seen is the object (Accusative). -ena would mean “by / with the man”.
The verb belongs at the end of the sentence.
One son, so the verb is singular: -ti matches putto, not the genitive narassa.

items: Endings, not word order, show a noun’s job.
Eight cases: Nominative, Vocative, Accusative, Instrumental, Ablative, Dative, Genitive, Locative.
A basic sentence is Subject (Nom.) + Object (Acc.) + Verb.
Verbs end in -ti for one and -nti for many.
Learn the shared endings (-assa, -ānaṃ, -ehi) and you have halved the work.
Neuter nouns only change in three cases.
